cards.explanation: The answer is that what has been decreed must be accomplished. That's the reason the text gives: he will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” Not a day past it. He does as he pleases, but he's still working on a clock he didn't set.

The answer is a god of fortresses. The text says the king honors “…a god of fortresses…” and it's a god his fathers did not know, honored with gold, silver, precious stones and riches. Big walls, big treasure, big price tag. I've honored my oven plenty, friends, but never with precious stones.

The answer is True. He will “…greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.” So there are rewards for the ones who side with him. It comes with a price tag, too, since the land is handed out for a price. I'd read that fine print twice, friends.

The answer is False. It's many countries, not one. The king of the North storms out with chariots, horsemen and many ships, “…invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood.” A flood doesn't stop at one backyard. That is a big, wide sweep.

The answer is Edom, Moab and the leaders of the Ammonites. The text says, “But these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.” Many countries fall when he invades the Beautiful Land, so those three being spared stands out. Notice it says the leaders of the Ammonites, not the whole country. Small detail, big difference.

The answer is False. Egypt does not escape. The text says, “He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape.” Egypt is named on purpose, so we can see how far his reach goes. Then the next verse says he gains control of its treasures of gold and silver.

The answer is that he goes out in great fury to destroy many. News from the east and the north alarms him, “…and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” He's alarmed, and then he goes out in fury. I think this is a heavy verse, friends.

The answer is False. No allies rush in. The text says “…he will meet his end with no one to help him.” That comes right after he pitches his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain. After all those countries, all those ships and all that gold, nobody steps in. I think that's a lonely spot to end up.

The answer is everyone whose name is written in the book. Michael, the great prince who stands watch over Daniel's people, will rise up. And at that time Daniel's people will be delivered, “…everyone whose name is found written in the book…” The key is the name in the book. Not a place, not a fight.

The answer is shame and everlasting contempt. Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, “…some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” I think this one is heavy, friends. Two ways to wake up, and the text names both.

The answer is those who lead many to righteousness. The text says “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Just before that, the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens. Stars are close to my heart, since every finished cookie box lights up my sky with one. Forever and ever is a long time to shine, friends.

The answer is to shut up the words and seal the book. Daniel is told, “But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” It's a book on hold, not a book thrown away. Then the text adds that many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase. So the words stay closed until the time of the end.

The answer is how long until these wonders are fulfilled. One of the two by the river says to the man dressed in linen, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” It's the kind of question we all want to ask. I've asked my oven the same thing, friends.

The answer is a time and times and half a time. The man dressed in linen swears by Him who lives forever, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” He raised both hands toward heaven to say it. It's the answer given, friends, even if it's not a date on a calendar.

The answer is False. Daniel says, “I heard, but I did not understand.” So he asks, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” Nothing shameful about it, friends. I once nodded at a recipe for ten minutes before admitting I had no idea what it meant.

The answer is True. Daniel is told, “None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.” That comes right after he hears that many will be purified, made spotless and refined. So understanding goes with the wise. The wicked don't get it.

The answer is that he will rest and then arise to his inheritance. The text says, “But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” After all those hard words, the last line is a gentle one. It's a good thing to hear at the end, friends.
